name: Kuwait

facts.religion: Muslim about 75% (citizens mostly Sunni with a Shia minority), large Christian and Hindu expatriate communities

snapshot: With parliament suspended, Kuwait's emir has stripped more than 71,000 people of citizenship and abolished naturalisation, redefining who counts as Kuwaiti.
leader: Emir Mishal al-Ahmad al-Jaber Al Sabah
culture: Kuwait's diwaniyas, evening gatherings in men's reception rooms, have long been the heart of social and political debate. Its TV dramas and theatre were once the most influential in the Gulf. The Kuwait Towers and Liberation Tower recall the oil boom and the 1990 Iraqi invasion, which remains a defining national memory.
society: Citizens, about a third of the population, enjoy generous state jobs, housing and subsidies funded by oil, while most residents are foreign workers. Tens of thousands of stateless Bidoon have long been denied citizenship. Kuwait's elected parliament was the most powerful in the Gulf until the emir suspended it in 2024.
situation: Kuwait was once the Gulf's experiment in democracy: since 1962 it has had the region's most powerful elected parliament, able to grill ministers and block budgets. Its citizens, about 1.5 million among a population of nearly five million, enjoy one of the world's most generous welfare states, funded by oil. In 2024 Emir Mishal al-Ahmad suspended parliament for up to four years, saying democracy was being abused. Since then he has been redefining who counts as Kuwaiti.

By 15 April 2026, more than 71,000 people had been stripped of citizenship, about 4.6 percent of all citizens, according to the Newsroom Initiative, which tracks official gazette decrees (New Lines). At least 26,000 of those affected are women who gained citizenship through marriage; others include former soldiers, doctors, athletes and artists. The government says it is correcting fraudulent naturalisations. A new decree-law in April restricted citizenship by origin to families present before 1920 and made nationality decisions "sovereign acts" beyond judicial review (bne IntelliNews). On 3 July further amendments abolished naturalisation altogether (ADHRB). The Iran war briefly paused the announcements, then they resumed within days of the April ceasefire, and in September another 415 people lost their nationality. The war also cut Kuwait's oil exports, which must pass through Hormuz, forcing its state oil company to declare force majeure. Critics who speak out have been summoned by state security.
power: A hereditary emirate ruled by the Al Sabah family. The emir appoints the crown prince and prime minister; the elected 50-seat National Assembly, normally one of the Gulf's strongest, has been suspended since May 2024, and the emir rules by decree.
holders: Emir Mishal al-Ahmad al-Jaber Al Sabah, since December 2023; Prime Minister Ahmad Abdullah al-Sabah.
